question: Hasn't evolution disproved Genesis, and with it the Christian story of creation and the fall?

ledger.heading: Thirteenth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the authors area, and the science area

shortAnswer: If its findings hold, evolution rules out some readings of Genesis, and it presses hard on questions Christians care about: death before human sin, and who Adam was. It hasn't disproved what the church confesses about creation. The creeds bind Christians to believe that God made all things, that human beings bear his image, that sin and death are real, and that Christ redeems. They don't bind anyone to an age of the earth or a mechanism of creation. Faithful Christians read Genesis in several ways: as six ordinary days not long ago, as long ages, as an account of God creating through evolution, and as a text whose days are a literary frame, God's workweek or the inauguration of a cosmic temple. Some also argue that features of life show design. This site takes no side among them. Each is held by people who confess the same faith, and each has a real difficulty, stated here.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
When Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* in 1859, he gave a natural account of the way living things fit their lives, the fact that had seemed for centuries the plainest sign of a designer. Richard Dawkins put the consequence in *The Blind Watchmaker* (1986): before Darwin an atheist could be consistent but had no explanation for the appearance of design, and after Darwin he had one.

The evidence has grown since. Jerry Coyne set it out for general readers in *Why Evolution Is True* (2009): the order of the fossil record, the distribution of species across the earth, organs that have lost their old use, and genes shared across species, broken ones among them, which he reads as marks of common ancestry. Mainstream science dates the universe at about 13.8 billion years and the earth at about 4.54 billion, and biology treats the common descent of living things, human beings included, as its settled framework. In 2008 the National Academy of Sciences and the Institute of Medicine published *Science, Evolution, and Creationism*, presenting evolution as well grounded in evidence and saying that accepting it can be compatible with religious faith.

The objection then turns to theology. If human beings descend from earlier creatures, there was death, predation and disease for hundreds of millions of years before any human sin. Genetic studies of human variation have been read as showing that our ancestors were never as few as two; the biologist Dennis Venema argued, in the chapters he wrote of *Adam and the Genome* (2017), a book shared with the theologian Scot McKnight, that the human population never fell below about ten thousand. Paul builds the gospel on Adam: "just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12, BSB). If there was no first man and death came long before sin, the objection says, the story of fall and redemption comes apart, and Christianity with it.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
The science should be stated at its strength and not disputed by insinuation. The age of the earth and the universe, and the common descent of living things, are the working consensus of the sciences that study them, held by researchers of every faith and none. A Christian who tells young people that these conclusions rest on little evidence, or that scientists are hiding what they know, misrepresents how those sciences hold their conclusions and why, and a young believer taught that the faith stands or falls with that claim may let go of both when she learns otherwise. That harm is real, and Christians have done it.

The theological questions are real too. Death before human sin, the suffering of animals over long ages, and the identity of Adam are not invented by skeptics. Christians who accept evolution feel them most, and the best of them say so.

sections.heading: The main Christian readings, and what they confess together
sections.body:
Here are the main readings, each in its defenders' terms, with its strongest point and its hardest difficulty. The site doesn't rank them.

Young-earth creation holds that God made the world in six ordinary days a few thousand years ago, that death entered the world through Adam's sin, and that the flood of Noah was global and laid down much of the geological record. Its modern form was revived by John Whitcomb and Henry Morris in *The Genesis Flood* (1961). Its strongest point is the text: the days are numbered and framed by evening and morning, and the Sabbath command grounds Israel's week in them, "For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested" (Exodus 20:11, BSB). It also keeps death as the enemy that came with sin. Its hardest difficulty is the evidence of geology, astronomy and biology, which the sciences read with near unanimity as showing a very old earth and the common descent of life. Some of its defenders state the size of that task plainly. The biochemist Todd Wood, a young-earth creationist, has written that the evidence for evolution is strong and that evolution is a successful theory, and holds to a young creation because of how he reads Scripture, not because he thinks the science is weak.

Old-earth creation holds that the universe and the earth are as old as mainstream science says, and that God created in stages over long ages, acting directly at points in the history of life. Its day-age form, defended by the astronomer Hugh Ross, who founded Reasons to Believe in 1986, reads each day as a long period, since the Hebrew word can mean a span of time, as in "the day that the LORD God made them" (Genesis 2:4, BSB). Its strongest point is that it accepts the evidence for the age of the world while keeping God's direct acts of creation within it. Its hardest difficulties come from both sides: the order of the days, with plants on the third before the sun on the fourth, fits a sequence of ages poorly, and the genetic evidence for common descent, humans included, is what mainstream biology finds most compelling.

Evolutionary creation holds that God created living things, human beings included, through the long process biology describes, and that Genesis teaches who made the world and why, not the method. Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project, founded BioLogos in 2007 to make this case. Its strongest point is that it accepts mainstream biology while keeping the confession of creation whole, and it stands in the old Christian teaching that God ordinarily works through the causes he made. Its hardest difficulty is the one the objection names: death and suffering over long ages before human sin, and what becomes of Adam and of Paul's argument in Romans 5.

Several readings concern what kind of text Genesis 1 is and can be held with more than one view of the science. The framework reading, proposed by Arie Noordtzij in 1924 and developed by Meredith Kline from 1958, holds that the days are a literary frame: three days of realms and three of their rulers. The analogical-day reading of C. John Collins (*Genesis 1-4*, 2006) holds that the days are God's workdays, like ours but not identical to them. John Walton's reading (*The Lost World of Genesis One*, 2009) holds that the seven days describe God establishing the cosmos as his temple, assigning functions rather than recounting material origins. Their strongest point is how much of the chapter's ancient shape they explain. Their shared difficulty is that Genesis 1 reads like a sequence, and Exodus 20:11 seems to take it as one.

Intelligent design is an argument, not a reading of Genesis. It holds that some features of living things are best explained by an intelligent cause rather than an unguided process. Michael Behe argued in *Darwin's Black Box* (1996) that some molecular machines, the bacterial flagellum his best-known example, are irreducibly complex, unable to work if any part is missing, and so unlikely to have been built step by step; Stephen Meyer argued in *Signature in the Cell* (2009) that the information in DNA is best explained by intelligence. By itself it names no designer and sets no age for the earth. Meyer argues that it is not an argument from ignorance: it infers design from what experience shows intelligent causes do. Its hardest difficulty is that mainstream biologists reject its central claims, and in *Kitzmiller v. Dover* (2005) a federal judge ruled that it could not be taught as an alternative to evolution in a public school's science classes. Some Christians press a theological worry as well. Deborah Haarsma, then president of BioLogos, granted that it isn't a god-of-the-gaps argument as such but argued that it shares that argument's risk: if research finds a natural cause, the inference falls.

Underneath the disagreement is the confession all of them share, and it is the part that matters most. God made all things: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1, BSB), and "By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command" (Hebrews 11:3, BSB). Human beings bear his image: "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Genesis 1:27, BSB). Sin and death are real, an enemy and not a design flaw, and they have come to all. And Christ redeems: "For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22, BSB). The Apostles' Creed confesses God the Father Almighty, "Maker of heaven and earth." It says nothing of how long the making took.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is a deductive argument about what evolution, if true, can and can't refute.
steps: What the church confesses about creation is that God made all things, that human beings bear his image, that sin and death are real, and that Christ redeems; the creeds don't confess an age of the earth or a mechanism of creation.
Each of the main Christian readings holds all four confessions without contradiction, and at least one of them, evolutionary creation, holds them while accepting the findings of evolutionary biology.
A finding that contradicts a reading of Genesis refutes that reading, not the confession it shares with the others.
sections.conclusion: So: evolution can't by itself refute Christianity's account of creation as the creeds confess it. It can refute particular readings, and its hardest pressure falls on questions within the confession, about death before sin and about Adam, which are real and are taken up below.
sections.after: The weight sits on the second step. A critic, and many Christians, will say that evolutionary creation can't hold the third and fourth confessions without contradiction, and that is the reply this page must answer.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply says the second step fails just where it matters. If death and suffering filled the world for ages before there were human beings, then God made the world through death, and death is not an enemy that came by sin. And if there was no single first pair, then Paul's argument in Romans 5, one man's sin and one man's obedience, has lost its first half. The young-earth reading keeps the doctrine by denying the science; evolutionary creation keeps the science by loosening the doctrine. Either way, Christianity loses something it can't afford.

This is the hardest question in the area, and it shouldn't be smoothed over. But Christians on every side of the science have given answers that keep the doctrine. On Adam, *Four Views on the Historical Adam* (2013) sets out the range: Denis Lamoureux argues there was no historical Adam, John Walton that Adam was historical but presented as an archetype, C. John Collins for a historical Adam with an old earth, and William Barrick for a historical Adam with a young earth. S. Joshua Swamidass argued in *The Genealogical Adam and Eve* (2019) that an Adam and Eve who lived as recently as six thousand years ago could be genealogical ancestors of everyone alive today without leaving a trace in our genes, a proposal its reviewers continue to test. On death, some read Paul in Romans 5 as speaking of human death, the death that came "to all men, because all sinned," and not of the death of every living thing. None of these answers is free of difficulty, and each is disputed by Christians as well as by skeptics. What they show is that the reply's dilemma isn't forced. A Christian can confess the fall and redemption without denying the science, and a Christian can reject the mainstream account of the earth's age and of common descent without being irrational about it. Neither choice abandons the creed.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: How to reconcile the long history of animal suffering with the goodness of creation is unresolved, and is part of the larger problem of natural evil. Who Adam was, when he lived and how he relates to the human population genetics describes is argued among Christians who all confess him; Venema's population estimate itself has been challenged, by Richard Buggs among others, and debated since. Whether intelligent design's arguments will hold up is contested. And on the extent of Noah's flood, global or regional, faithful readers also differ, and this site takes no side.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Christians differ on the age of the earth, on evolution, on the details of a historical Adam and on the extent of the flood, and the site takes no position on any of them. These are questions on which faithful churches differ without dividing the faith. A Christian who changes her mind about the age of the earth hasn't changed her religion. The Genesis 1 note in the Study Bible sets out the readings of the days, and the page "How should a Christian read Genesis 1?" gives each its strongest case. Todd Wood and the biologist Darrel Falk, a former president of BioLogos, wrote *The Fool and the Heretic* (2019) out of a long dialogue with each other; its subtitle speaks of moving beyond labels to a Christian dialogue about creation and evolution, and they still disagree. That is the spirit this page asks for. What none of them may give up is the confession: God made all things, we bear his image, sin and death are real, and Christ redeems.
